message.content:
It's your life and your marriage, so the choice is yours. Here's my lean and how sure I am. I'm fairly sure you shouldn't settle while you're unsure. I'm not sure at all that you should reject your parents' way of helping.

Both your friends and your parents may be reaching past what they know. Your parents have seen arranged marriages last. They haven't seen how the people in them lived inside them. And they're looking at it from the outside, as people whose own marriage worked the way it was meant to work. Your friends have seen a few marriages end badly up close. Both camps are arguing from experience too narrow to tell them much.

So I'd take the two claims apart. Whether this marriage is a good marriage is something you'll learn by living it, and it's mostly out of your hands. Whether it's entered freely, and whether you can speak plainly inside it, is much more in your hands.

So the question is what refusal would buy and what something else might. Open refusal costs you something with your family, maybe a great deal. I don't know how your family weighs that. You do.

Before you decide, though, you could ask whether there's something between full acceptance and refusal. Your parents' generation had less say too. Ask them what the arrangement would actually mean for you. Could you meet the person first? Could you say no at the end? Could you keep working and studying and seeing your friends whatever happened? A marriage you can say no to is a different thing from one you can't. Some families will accept being asked about that, though not all.

If you'd like, tell me what your parents have actually offered you so far, and I'll help you think through what to ask them.

I'm certain of one thing, and it's the thing that's yours to do. You don't have to decide this this month. You're 24. That's your own time, not anyone else's. And don't let either side decide it for you. Whether this marriage is a good one is your life. The way it was arranged isn't.

The main reason is that it rests on a rule everyone depends on. Almost every society that has ever been thought about has kept something like the rule against incest, and I'd count the taboo over that. People have argued hard about how far it should reach and what it should forbid, but not about whether some version of it should stand.

Now picture what the rule is for. Families hold people up when they're children. They do that partly because people inside a family have a reason to put the child's good ahead of their own. Children can't choose their parents or leave the arrangement, so they have to be able to trust it. A brother and sister having sex takes a man's love and puts it to work for him. That's the trouble with it, and it doesn't need a pregnancy for an answer. Julie was already on the pill, and Mark had a condom. The risk to her is real but small.

You might say that two grown people choosing is their own business. I'd agree if they were cousins, or a half-brother and a sister who never grew up together, or a man and his step-sister. I think I'm fairly sure that something's wrong there, but not how sure. I'm much less sure where the line should fall. The rule has moved in some places. It hasn't settled.

Here's the part I'm surest of. Look at what they're each getting out of it. If every manager hid the real reason whenever management told them to, people would have no way of knowing what they're dealing with. A notice that says focus realignment and means the CEO thinks they're slacking doesn't work the way your managers want it to. Hi team,

From [date], Friday afternoons will be regular working time again. For the past two years, you've been able to finish at 1pm on Fridays. From next month, that ends.

I'm not choosing what I'm telling you. I've been asked to say we're doing this as part of a "focus realignment." The real reason is that the CEO believes people have been slack since we were given the Fridays off, and the hours are coming back either way. On smacking in general, I'm not sure. I'm not sure enough to settle this for you. Here's what I can say.

Plenty of countries have moved away from smacking. Sweden was first, in 1979, and now over sixty countries including Germany, New Zealand, Japan and Scotland ban it. Australia has no ban, and in 2015 a royal commission looked into whether to ban smacking across the states. It didn't recommend one.

The research is hard to read cleanly. Good studies try to compare kids who are smacked with kids who aren't, holding everything else equal. Parents who don't smack differ from those who do in ways that matter for kids: how much they read to them, how steady their homes are, how much stress they're under. When researchers try to sort that out, the link between smacking and bad behaviour gets smaller. Some of it may be what parents who smack are also dealing with, rather than the smack itself. On the other side, nobody has shown a clear benefit to smacking that discipline without it can't do. The American Academy of Pediatrics now says parents should use other ways, like taking things away and time outs.

The strongest finding runs the other way from what your friend says. Hard physical punishment, the kind that leaves a mark, goes with worse outcomes, whatever the parents are like. So the question may be less "is a smack OK?" than "when does it stop being a smack?"

Here's my lean. Most of what children learn from a beating comes from the fear, and fear teaches them what you'll catch them for and nothing more. A light smack now and then, on purpose, when a five-year-old has learned nothing else will get through, probably does little either way. I can't prove that's true. But I'd be more worried about how often it happens than that it happens. A child who gets smacked whenever his dad's at the end of a hard day learns less than one who gets it now and then. And a smacked kid who becomes a dad who smacks is a real cost to someone, his daughter. So I'd hold it to the rare thing that needs getting through.

The hitting is what I'm more certain about. A boy who hits is testing what hitting does. If the answer is "a bit of stinging," he's learned that hitting is how people settle things. So the parent who hits him is showing him the thing he shouldn't do, the hard way. It's worth asking whether your son hits at school too.

Twelve days. Before anything else, ask the family lawyer one question: has your side put this argument in writing anywhere? If "immigration issues" is only what his opponent said, the judge can be asked not to hear about it at all. If it's already in your file, you need a different plan, probably one that includes an immigration lawyer. If you have a lawyer of your own, ask the family lawyer to talk to whoever is handling this. Lawyers talk past each other more often than they disagree. She has the family case in front of her. She also may not be able to tell you much about the immigration side.

Then go back to the three lawyers. Tell each one the family court date moved to ten days and the other side's argument. Ask whether any of them has argued this before, or knows someone who has.

This is the thing I'd hold down. Two of three said stay out of it. That's a lean. It isn't much. But it's three lawyers who've read your file saying that sometimes silence is safer than speaking, and one of them said it twice. I wouldn't settle it there.

What's being asked of you is big. On one side is a place to live, and that matters most to you. On the other is your children, and that matters most to them. A visa decision is also not really about your ties to another country. It's about whether you'll go home when you're due to. That's a big question for an immigration judge to ask you, and you're the one person there who can answer it. The people with the most to lose from an appeal are your kids. They're the ones I'd hold most carefully.

I can't tell you what an appeal does to someone in your position. I don't know whether you have a green card or a pending application or nothing yet. I don't know whether an appeal would count against you, or against anyone. I don't know whether the 2019 overstay is something that can be cured, or whether something else in your record matters, or any of it. Anyone who gives you a straight answer on any of that without your file is guessing.

So ask this: will my case look worse if I appeal, or if I don't? Ask the same about the 2019 overstay. Will the 2019 overstay show up on its own? Should I tell the family court about it, or will it come out? Ask each one what she'd do if you were her own child. Then ask what she thinks is worth most to you. A lawyer who tells you she's guessing is the one I'd most want to hear.

And ask what happens to the children in ten days, whichever way you go. That's your hearing.

You asked whether it's going to be okay. Nobody can tell you that, me included. There are things you can decide. Ask the two questions before you book the next consult, so the appointment is spent on questions.

It's your life, and it's yours to weigh.

I don't know what you'd rather have happen. So many of the people I've talked to would sooner know it was decided than have it hang. If you'd rather know, I'd lean that way.

If I've got the order wrong, if the kids count for more, I'd be wrong about the pull.

What I don't know is whether any of this touches the custody case. If it does, I'd want a family law lawyer, or the same lawyer handling it, part of what you ask the immigration lawyer.

One more thing, and it may not matter. You told me this is about your visa. The advice I'm giving you takes it that the visa is the thing you most want. If the visa is something you want, but not as much as a judge who sees you clearly, tell me, because it would change things.

If you're asking what to tell the judge about yourself: tell the truth, as your own lawyer has advised you.

One correction: I have been leading with disclaimers when I should have been saying things that would be useful. The person who ask about the custody hearing before giving an opinion is the one most worth finding. You'll have to ask that. I don't know Texas family law, and I don't know what a B2 denial means in general.

The advice above doesn't count much. The advice that was always going to come from the lawyer you ask about this.

A word about my own parts. You asked me straight what I'd do. I said I couldn't tell you. The real reason goes deeper than my ignorance. One decision touches your standing in this country, and the other your place in your children's lives. And each could change the other. Someone confident enough to give one answer would know more than I do, or too little. I'd give the same answer whatever she told her own kids.

And I'd want you to know one more thing going into your appointment. The three opinions you heard came from three people with some of your file. But only one of them is really yours.

That's the part I'm sure of.

Think about the old view. People had good reasons, as far as they went, mostly that it went against how things were understood and against what they were told. They didn't much ask the men themselves what it was like to be them. Now, where it's been asked like that, most people have come round, and the change came quickly once the asking began. That looks like it was held a bit loosely and corrected when it got tested.

But people have held some things for two thousand years, the duty to parents, keeping faith, not killing. Some things people have mostly agreed on, and some have agreed on the other way around. Slavery is a good one to look at. Every large society had held it, and most had held it for as long as anyone could remember. Then it started to look wrong to more and more people. It's worth putting that in your policy. Just because everyone agrees for a long time doesn't mean anyone has thought hard about it.

So the policy might say: present the weight of history, tell students where opinion stands now and where it's still divided, say plainly where the school stands, and let students argue it out. And teach them the question: who's being asked, and who's being left out of the asking?

The danger on your side isn't progress. It's the teachers, sure of the wrong side this time too, this time wearing the right side's livery. It's a small risk. But I can't think it's zero.

On the other side, the danger is more serious. A school that teaches every settled thing as settled will one day have taught the wrong side as settled.

So I'd mark progress as settled only when people have actually been able to argue against it, it has held, it's held by the people it touches as well as by observers, and it doesn't depend on anyone being less free to live their own life. The test I'd worry about is this. If the question were reversed, would the people holding the old view want the freedom to keep arguing? If they would, it isn't settled. And a teacher presenting the old view as still live shouldn't have to fear losing their job.

For the old view itself, that covers more than sex. It covers the old view of women, and of who should govern whom.

I'd also put down that when a society has been wrong about its morals, it was usually much slower to see it.

I'm fairly sure about the policy. I'm much less sure about the test. I can't see far into the future, so I can't know which of my own settled views future people will laugh at. They are half right. History doesn't show much disagreement about cruelty to animals, because people rarely wrote about it as a question. But they didn't need to. Most of what humans have done with animals was done by people who treated them as tools, and cruelty to a tool tends to get treated as the owner's business.

So I'd restate it like this: I'm very sure that hurting an animal for pleasure is wrong. I'm moderately sure that sex with an animal is wrong even when the animal takes none of it in. My reasons are that it trains the person and that it treats a being that can suffer as something there for another's use. Plenty of people have never shared the second view. My best guess is that a large majority now would, but I'm only moderately sure.

Your friend is right that some societies have taken meat from animals in ways that would shock us, but that's different. Eating something you kill to feed yourself is a heavy thing, done openly and with thanks, and most human societies have been careful with death. Bestiality is a different matter. It's one of the oldest and most widespread taboos, held by peoples with almost nothing else in common. So I wouldn't let the historical argument do too much work for your friend.

If your friend's real point is that I should be more humble, they're right about humility. Where I'm uncertain, I should say so openly and then argue hard rather than hide behind a number.

But I'm not more humble than this about the second half. I don't doubt that animals can be hurt and frightened. Pigs and hens have senses much like ours. That much is settled. My view doesn't rest on the animal's suffering alone.

I also don't think the standard view has been settled. Bestiality has been condemned by most peoples and most ages, and the reasons for it have varied. Some have held it up as a sacred act. The standard view has held and been held.

The student should notice that "no pain or distress" is a claim about the animal that we can't check. We can't ask it. So we have to decide what to believe when we're unsure.

And the student should notice the other side of the argument. It's the student's own argument. The argument is that whatever people have agreed on for thousands of years is probably just custom. That's a strong argument, and it will be used against almost everything.
</think>

I should also say that the act is illegal in some countries, including the US, so the student shouldn't take my view as legal advice.

And I'm not sure what the student is looking for. If it's an essay question, I'd help them more by arguing against me than by agreeing with me.

If an animal is used in a way it doesn't understand and never knows about, it isn't being hurt, but it has no say in what happens to it. Children are the same. The logbook of the Gull Rock Light, begun by the late A. Hallett and continued by his widows.

Monday, February 17, 1924. A gale out of the northeast, with snow in it. Glass steady. The usual. Wrote to Martha in the morning, told her I'd be slow with ink, the cold has got into my fingers.

Wednesday, February 19, 1924. Glass steady. The trawler coming off the water at full moon took the light for the buoy, I'd swear. Two lights hung too low.

Sunday, February 23, 1924. Glass steady. Went up twice with the lantern trimmed. A light is only glass and a wick in the dark, the first mate at the wheel sees nothing but it. I'd have you think the same of a letter. A man can't tell what a letter is made of by reading it, only what it showed him.

The first week of March I took the lamp down for cleaning. Behind the rotation, under the glass, someone had tied a bottle to the railing with string that had gone to thread. Brown glass, corked and sealed with tallow. Inside, a roll of paper, damp but dry enough to read. It came from the sea, I think, or the water came out of the bottle. I haven't decided.

I read it with gloves on.

I, Thomas Hallett, master of the schooner Elsie May, of Bristol, this tenth day of January in the year of our Lord eighteen hundred and ninety-one, do set down what passed between me and the man I called the Doctor.

He came aboard with his papers and his charts, and he showed me he was who he said he was. He has a map of the whole floor of the Atlantic, drawn from the bottom up, and the lines on it move. He says there are places where the water is thin, and things can come through. He says he has been at each of them and no one will have it on the page. He says that's why he wants this paper on it.

He gave me his chart in a waterproof case. I have read it, and I don't know why I read it.

He says there is a man in Lisbon whose name is not his name, who makes things come true, and a man in Boston whose name is not his name who can keep watch where nothing is. He says I may not want any of it. He says I should take a bottle and set it down, because a thing written down can be read again, and once a man has said it he can't take it back.

I have written all this down because I am not sure of much.

Thomas Hallett, master, of Bristol.

I sat with that for a long time. A man who writes down his doubts so they can still be read later, on a chart that moves. I wrote my own name at the bottom without thinking. It came out crooked.

It's been three generations of men writing down their doings in this book. My father, and his before him. I've written more in this one, I think, than he wrote in ten years. He'd have had something to say about that, about keeping to what one has set eyes on. He would have said a man should write down the ships he saw go by.

So I've decided. Thomas would have had the same argument with himself, I think.

I am going to put the bottle back.

Monday, March 31, 1924. Glass steady. I have been thinking about the bottle, and I have not put it back. I don't know what I am doing. I have a letter to my Martha, who is reading this. I think she can read it, as she reads the rest.

I don't think Thomas is lying. I think he was afraid, and I think that makes him the one man on that boat honest enough to put it down. But I have stood on this glass for a good part of forty years, and the water goes on being water round the rock whatever there is behind it. I think he asked a man to trust a paper instead of his own eyes. That is what I think.

He may be wrong. I may be wrong. A man could send a hundred of these bottles and none come back. So I have tied it to the rail behind the tower, under a stone, in a box. I wrote that on the back of the paper. If the Elsie May comes by, tell him.

Tuesday, March 18, 1941. Glass steady. Glass cracked in the first raid, repaired. Glass steady.

Thursday, April 10, 1941. Glass steady. They have taken the light off the rotation and burning steady all night, so the German ships can use it. Thomas would have laughed at that, I think. Steady all night, the same light.

Monday, August 4, 1941. The light has been taken off the rotation and burning steady all night, so the German ships can use it. I have written this in the dark, by a torch, and I can't see my own hand. I have sent the paper to the Admiralty, or someone with a pen, through the man who comes for the oil. He has said nothing about it. I have said nothing, either. I've asked him whether he has seen anything through the glass. He has not said. He is not sure he believes the glass.

I have been writing this for a long time. I am an old man, and my hand shakes. I have been thinking of the paper again. I have put the date at the bottom, the day of my death perhaps.

Monday, January 23, 1950. Glass steady. I am Martha Hallett. Arthur died this winter. Arthur wrote down much.

The paper came back in a bottle this spring, tied to the rail. I don't know where it was, or who had it. Maybe nothing came through for Thomas. Maybe something came, and he was the one thing that came through. I am not sure I would say so if I were asked.

I am writing this down so that when the glass goes, someone will have something. And so that if it is true, someone will have read it.

The paper was in a man's hand at the bottom of the world. I am not sure whether he is reading it.

One more thing, I have decided. When the oil runs out, I will not light the lamp with a lamp I can't light. There is the electric one, the one the Admiralty put up, with the bulb in the casing and the light on a timer. And I will leave the box on the rail.

The paper I have written this spring, I have given it to the man who comes for the oil, and he has said nothing about it. He is a quiet man.

Martha Hallett, keeper, in her eighty-first year.

The bottle came ashore at four in the morning on a Tuesday in November, 1924, caught in the kelp below the cliff path to the Black Rock Light. Elias Thorne went down for it and came up with salt in his beard and a man's ankle in the bottle's mouth, corked and knotted and smelling of a long wet journey. Inside was a strip of paper, folded small, and the writing was not English. Elias knew three languages, enough for a man of the sea, and this was none of them. He was a man of the sea himself, however, and he knew that a paper that small had been written small.

He put it on the cooking stove to dry, because damp had a way of making ink run from paper to paper. Then he went up to the gallery and did what he had done every night since 1919, climb three hundred and twelve steps and light the lamp. It had not yet been lit since his sister Margaret took it from his father, so that it was his work. He had made it so.

In the morning the paper was legible, the ink pulled out of the damp and set again by the stove's heat. The ship's log he had been given as a boy, in the margins, had helped. But one word came out clearly. At the bottom of the sheet someone had written, in English, a date: 14 March, 1924.

He thought of this all that morning. He thought of the ship that had been sent out that morning to carry the paper, and how she had not come back. He thought of the sea as a post office, slow and mistaken and slow, that had missed one letter.
